fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is God’s own power at work to save everyone who believes, the Jew first and the Greek as well. In it the righteousness of God is being revealed, from faith for faith. As it is written, “The one who is righteous will live by faith.”

— Romans 1:16–17

Some time around AD 57, in the port city of Corinth, Paul sat down with a secretary named Tertius and dictated the longest letter he ever wrote. It was addressed to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the world, and it was carried there by a woman from the harbour town of Cenchreae named Phoebe.

No one in Corinth could have guessed what it would become. Few pieces of writing have been argued over, preached from and prayed through more. Augustine was converted reading it. Luther found the gospel again in it. Wesley felt his heart “strangely warmed” while someone read aloud a preface to it. Calvin called it a doorway into the whole of Scripture.

And yet it is a letter, not a textbook. It begins with greetings and ends with a list of friends. Between the two, Paul argues, pleads, asks himself questions and answers them, breaks off into praise, and grieves for his own people. To read it well is to hear a man thinking aloud, with all his heart, about what God has done in Jesus Christ.

A letter to a church Paul had never visited

Paul did not found the church in Rome, and no one knows who did. There were visitors from Rome in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and believers travelling the roads of the empire probably carried the news home. By the time Paul wrote, people throughout the world, he says, were speaking of its faith.

It was a church of Jews and Gentiles together, and that was not always easy. The Roman historian Suetonius records that the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome (probably around AD 49), and Acts tells of Aquila and his wife Priscilla, Paul’s Prisca, arriving in Corinth because of it (Acts 18:2). When Jewish believers returned after Claudius died in 54, they would have found congregations grown largely Gentile in their absence. Many readers think that lies behind the letter’s refrain, “the Jew first and the Greek as well”, and behind its plea in chapters 14 and 15 for believers who disagree about food and holy days to welcome one another.

Paul gives his own reasons near the end (15:22–33). His work in the east is done, “from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum” (15:19). He is about to take a gift from the Gentile churches of Greece to the poor believers in Jerusalem; after that he means to go west, to Spain, and to visit Rome on the way. He wants the Roman church to know him, to pray for him, and to help him on his way. So he sets out, more fully than anywhere else, the gospel he preaches.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–4: the gospel of God’s righteousness. Every human being, Jew and Gentile alike, stands guilty before God; God declares people righteous as a free gift, through faith in Jesus Christ; and Abraham shows that it was always so.
  • Chapters 5–8: the new life. Peace with God; Adam and Christ; dying and rising with Christ; the struggle with sin and the law; and life in the Spirit, which nothing can take away.
  • Chapters 9–11: Israel and the nations. If God’s promises were made to Israel, and most of Israel has not believed, has God’s word failed?
  • Chapters 12–16: a people shaped by mercy. Bodies offered as a living sacrifice, love in practice, the strong and the weak, Paul’s plans, and his greetings.

Each part leans on the one before. The commands of chapter 12 begin with a “so”, and that “so” rests on eleven chapters of God’s mercy.

All have sinned

Paul begins not with good news but with bad. From 1:18 to 3:20 he builds a case, and every reader is meant to find himself in it. First the Gentile world, which knew enough of God to thank him and did not, and “traded the truth about God for the lie”. Then, turning on anyone who has been nodding along, the moral person who judges others and does the same things. Then his own people, who have the law and the covenant and are no less in need. The case closes with a chain of quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah: “No one is righteous, not even one.”

This is not gloom for its own sake. If everyone is in the same condition, then everyone can be met by the same grace. The verdict and the remedy come in a single sentence:

Everyone has sinned, and all come short of God’s glory. Yet they are declared righteous as a free gift, by his grace, through the redemption found in Christ Jesus.

— Romans 3:23–24

Righteousness from God, through faith

“But now”, Paul writes at 3:21, and the whole letter turns. God’s righteousness has come to light apart from the law, “through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe.” God put Christ forward as the means of atonement, by his blood, so that he would be both righteous himself and “the one who declares righteous whoever has faith in Jesus.”

This is what Christians call justification by faith. The Greek verb belongs to the law court: it is a judge’s verdict, declaring someone in the right. Paul’s astonishing claim is that God gives that verdict to the guilty, not for anything they have done, but as a free gift received by trusting him. God is the God “who declares the ungodly righteous” (4:5), and boasting is shut out.

Christians have understood this in more than one way. Catholic and Orthodox readers stress that the God who declares righteous also makes righteous; the Reformers stressed that the verdict rests wholly on Christ, received by faith alone, and that the new life flows from it rather than earning it. More recently, E. P. Sanders reassessed the Judaism of Paul’s day, and James Dunn and N. T. Wright have argued that “works of the law” means especially the marks that set Jews apart from Gentiles, so that Paul’s first concern is who belongs to God’s people; others answer that his argument reaches deeper, to the impossibility of anyone earning God’s favour. The letter itself is the best place to weigh them.

To show that none of this is new, Paul turns in chapter 4 to Abraham, the father of Israel:

“Abraham believed God, and that was counted to him as righteousness.”

— Romans 4:3

Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, Paul points out, so he is father both of Jews who believe and of Gentiles who believe. His faith was no vague optimism. He was about a hundred years old, and he trusted the God “who brings the dead to life and calls into being things that do not exist.” That is the God, Paul says, who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

Adam and Christ

Chapter 5 opens with the fruit of all this: “we are at peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” And it gives the deepest reason for that peace:

But God proves how much he loves us: Christ died for us when we were still sinners.

— Romans 5:8

Then Paul steps back to take in the whole of human history. Through one man, Adam, sin and death came into the world. Through one man, Jesus Christ, came the free gift and life. The two are alike in shape and utterly unlike in size: “where sin multiplied, grace overflowed far beyond it.” Christians have drawn on this passage in thinking about original sin, and differed over it. But Paul’s emphasis falls on the second man. The point is not how far we fell, but how much further grace reaches.

Dead to sin, alive to God

If grace is so abundant, someone objects, why not go on sinning? “Certainly not!” Those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death and buried with him, so that they might “live a life that is new.” Paul’s picture is a change of masters: once slaves of sin, now slaves of righteousness, and of God.

Chapter 7 turns to the law. It is holy, Paul insists, and its commandment “holy, just and good”, and yet it could not give life. Then come some of the most personal words he ever wrote: “The things I want to do, I fail to do; the things I hate are what I end up doing.” And at the end, the cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who will set me free from this body of death?”

Who is the “I” of Romans 7? Christians have never fully agreed. Augustine in his later years, and Luther and Calvin after him, heard the believer, still fighting the sin that remains. Others, from Chrysostom to many interpreters today, hear the person under the law without the Spirit, described with Christian hindsight. Either way, the chapter ends not in despair but in thanksgiving: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

No sentence of condemnation

Many readers count Romans 8 the greatest chapter in the Bible. It begins:

So then, those who are in Christ Jesus now face no sentence of condemnation.

— Romans 8:1

It is the chapter of the Spirit. The Spirit gives life where the law could not; the Spirit leads God’s children and testifies that they belong to him; in the Spirit they call out “Abba, Father!” The whole creation groans, waiting for God’s children to be revealed, and so do believers, and the Spirit himself pleads for them “with groans that no words carry.”

Then, in rising questions, Paul gathers everything up. “If God is on our side, who can stand against us?” Who will accuse? Who will condemn? Who can tear us away from the love of Christ? The answer is the peak of the letter’s first half:

For I am fully persuaded that not death and not life, not angels and not rulers, not what is here now and not what is yet to come, not any powers, not what is high above and not what is deep below, nor any other created thing, will be able to cut us off from God’s love, which is ours in Christ Jesus our Lord.

— Romans 8:38–39

Israel and the nations

Readers sometimes treat chapters 9 to 11 as a detour. Paul does not. Straight after the joy of chapter 8 he speaks of the constant pain in his heart for his own people, most of whom have not believed in their Messiah. If God’s promises to Israel could fail, how could anyone trust the promises of chapter 8?

His answer moves in stages. God’s word has not failed, because God has always worked by choosing, by mercy and not by human striving. Israel has stumbled, pursuing righteousness as though it came by works; yet “all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved.” And God has not rejected his people: there is a remnant, chosen by grace, and Paul is one of them. Gentile believers are wild olive shoots grafted into Israel’s tree, and must not boast over the natural branches, which God can graft back in. A hardening has come upon part of Israel “until the full number of the Gentiles comes in. And in this way all Israel will be saved.”

These chapters are read in very different ways. In the tradition of Augustine and Calvin, chapter 9 teaches God’s choice of individuals for salvation; in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, it speaks of God choosing peoples and persons for a part in his purpose, with salvation resting on a faith open to all. “All Israel” has been read as the Jewish people turning to Christ at the last, as the whole people of God, or as all believing Israel through history. Every reading must keep where Paul lands: “the gifts and the call of God can never be taken back”, and God has locked everyone up in disobedience “so that he may show mercy to everyone.” Then Paul stops arguing and worships.

A living sacrifice

The last part of the letter turns all of this into a way of life:

So, brothers and sisters, I appeal to you by the mercies of God: offer your bodies to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to him. That is your reasonable worship.

— Romans 12:1

What follows is practical, and searching. Believers are one body with many gifts. Their love is to be real, with no pretense. They are to bless those who persecute them, weep with those who weep, never avenge themselves, and feed their enemies: “Do not let evil defeat you; defeat evil with good.” Chapter 13 speaks of the governing authorities, a passage argued over in times of peace and of persecution alike, and of the one debt never paid off, the debt of love.

Chapters 14 and 15 come down to the dinner table. Some believers eat anything; others eat only vegetables. Some keep special days; others treat every day alike. Paul’s concern is that no one despise or judge another, since each belongs to the Lord: “So welcome one another, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.” The great doctrines end in a church where Jews and Gentiles, the strong and the weak, sit down and eat together.

A real church

Romans 16 is the chapter most readers skip, and it is worth slowing down for. Paul commends Phoebe, “a deacon of the church in Cenchreae” and a patron to many. Then he greets twenty-six people in Rome, twenty-four of them by name, and nine of them women: Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for him; Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with him and are “prominent among the apostles”; Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis, who have worked hard in the Lord; Rufus’s mother, “who has also been a mother to me.” Several of the names were common among slaves and freed slaves. There is a church that meets in a house.

The great argument was read aloud to small congregations of ordinary people, men and women, slave and free, Jew and Gentile, and here they are greeted one by one.

Romans in the life of the church

John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter at Antioch in the fourth century, said he heard Paul’s letters read twice every week, and was warmed each time, as if by the voice of a friend.

In a garden in Milan in 386, Augustine heard a child’s voice saying “Take up and read.” He opened Paul’s letters, and his eyes fell on the end of Romans 13:

Let us live decently, as people do in the daytime: not in wild parties and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and shameless excess, not in quarrels and envy. Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ like clothing, and do not make plans to satisfy the desires of the flesh.

— Romans 13:13–14

He tells us in his Confessions that he read no further, nor needed to: the darkness of doubt was gone.

Eleven centuries later Martin Luther, teaching at Wittenberg, wrestled with “the righteousness of God” in 1:17. He had heard it as the righteousness by which God punishes sinners, and he hated it. When at last he understood it as the righteousness God gives, by which “the one who is righteous will live by faith”, he felt, he said, that he had been born again and had entered paradise through open gates. In his preface to the letter he called Romans the chief part of the New Testament and the purest gospel.

And on the evening of 24 May 1738, at a meeting in Aldersgate Street in London, John Wesley listened as someone read from that preface. “About a quarter before nine,” he wrote, “while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed.” Wesley’s preaching in the revival that followed flowed out of that evening.

How to read Romans

Read it through once, in a sitting or two, to hear it as the Roman Christians did, aloud and all at once. Then read it slowly.

Notice Paul’s questions. Again and again he raises an objection (“What then are we to say?”, “Is the law sin?”) and answers it, often with “Certainly not!” He is anticipating his hearers’ questions, and yours. Notice his “so” and “therefore”: Romans is an argument, and its conclusions stand on what comes before. Notice how often he breaks into praise, at the end of chapter 8, of chapter 11, and of the letter. And do not stop at chapter 11. The letter is not finished until the doctrine has sat down at table.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Romans are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Declared righteous.” Where older Bibles say “justified”, this translation says what the word means in a court: God “declares righteous”. It keeps “righteous” and “righteousness” throughout, so that a reader can follow one family of words, plainly related in Greek, through the whole argument.

“Faith in Jesus Christ.” The Greek of 3:22 says literally “faith of Jesus Christ”. It can mean faith that has Jesus as its object, or Jesus’ own faithfulness to God, shown in his death. This translation follows the first reading, and its notes give the second, which many scholars hold.

“Flesh.” Where Paul means human life under the sway of sin, set against the Spirit, as in chapters 7 and 8, the translation keeps “flesh”, so that the contrast can be seen. Where he simply means descent, as when Christ is born of David’s line (1:3), it says “by human descent”.

Places where manuscripts differ. In 16:7 it reads Junia, a woman’s name, as early Christian writers did. In 5:1 it reads “we are at peace with God”; many early manuscripts have “let us have peace”, a difference of one vowel. And the closing praise (16:25–27), which stands in different places in different manuscripts, is printed at the end, where most Bibles have it.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, but it is worth remembering, especially in chapters 9 to 11, that the word means Israel’s anointed King.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Romans 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God. God promised this gospel long ago through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. It concerns his Son, who by human descent was born of the line of David, and who was appointed Son of God in power, through the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection of the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord. Through him we have received grace and apostleship, to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations for the sake of his name. You are among them, you whom Jesus Christ has called to be his own. To all of you in Rome whom God loves and has called to be his holy people: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul longs to visit Rome

To begin with, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for every one of you, because people throughout the whole world are speaking of your faith. God, whom I serve with my whole spirit in proclaiming the gospel of his Son, can testify how constantly I remember you in my prayers. I am always asking that somehow, if God wills it, the way may at last be opened for me to come to you. I long to see you so that I can share some spiritual gift with you that will make you strong. What I mean is that, while I am with you, we will be encouraged together by each other’s faith, yours and mine. I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that I have often planned to come to you, so that I might gather some harvest among you too, as I have among the other Gentiles, but until now I have been kept from coming. I am under obligation to Greeks and to non-Greeks, to the educated and to the uneducated. So, for my part, I am eager to bring the gospel to you in Rome as well.

The power of the gospel

I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is God’s own power at work to save everyone who believes, the Jew first and the Greek as well. In it the righteousness of God is being revealed, from faith for faith. As it is written, “The one who is righteous will live by faith.”

Humanity turns from the Creator

God’s wrath is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wrongdoing of people who by their wrongdoing hold down the truth. For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God himself has made it plain to them. Since the world was made, what cannot be seen of God, his everlasting power and divine nature, has been in plain view, understood from the things he made. So they have no excuse. Although they knew God, they did not give him glory as God or thank him. Their reasoning turned to emptiness, and darkness filled their senseless hearts. They claimed to be wise, but they became fools. They traded the glory of the God who never dies for images made to look like mortal human beings, or birds, or beasts, or creatures that crawl.

So God handed them over, in the cravings of their hearts, to impurity, and they dishonored their bodies with one another. They traded the truth about God for the lie. They bowed down to the creation and served it, instead of the one who created it, who is blessed forever. Amen.

That is why God handed them over to passions that bring dishonor. Their women gave up natural sexual use for what goes against nature. The men did the same: they left behind natural relations with women and were set on fire with craving for one another. Males with males, they did what is shameless, and they received in themselves the fitting penalty for their straying.

And since they did not think God worth acknowledging, God handed them over to a worthless mind, and so they do things that should never be done. Every kind of wrongdoing fills them: wickedness, greed, malice. They are brimming with envy, murder, rivalry, deceit and spite. They whisper about others and speak against them; they hate God; they treat others with contempt; they are proud and full of boasting; they think up new evils; they defy their parents; they are without sense, without loyalty, without love, without mercy. They know God’s just decree, that people who do such things deserve to die, yet they not only do them but cheer on others who do them.

fields.title: Romans 2
fields.body_html:
God judges without favor

So you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you pass judgment on others. In judging someone else you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, do the very same things. We know that God’s judgment on those who do such things rests on the truth. When you judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, do you really think you will escape God’s judgment? Or do you make light of how rich he is in kindness, tolerance and patience? Do you not see that God is kind to you in order to bring you to repentance? But your heart is hard and will not repent, and so you are piling up wrath for yourself against the day of wrath, when God will make his righteous judgment known. He will give each person what their deeds deserve. Those who persist in doing good, seeking glory, honor and immortality, he will reward with eternal life. But for those who are driven by selfish ambition, who reject the truth and follow wrongdoing instead, there will be wrath and fury. There will be trouble and anguish for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek. But there will be glory, honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek. For God does not favor one person over another.

The law and those without it

Those who sin without having the law will be lost without the law, and those who sin while living under the law will be judged by the law. Hearing the law does not make anyone righteous before God; those who do what the law says are the ones God will declare righteous. Gentiles do not have the law. Yet when, by nature, they carry out what the law says, they become their own law, though the law was never given to them. Their conduct shows that the work of the law is written in their hearts. Their conscience bears witness too, and their thoughts argue with one another, now accusing them, now defending them, on the day when God, through Christ Jesus, judges the hidden things in people’s lives, as the gospel I preach says.

Teaching others, not yourself

Now you call yourself a Jew. You rely on the law and take pride in God. You know his will, and because the law has taught you, you can tell what matters most. You are sure that you can guide the blind and be a light to people in the dark, one who corrects the foolish and teaches the young, because in the law you have the very shape of knowledge and truth. So you teach others; will you not teach yourself? You preach that people should not steal; do you steal? You say that people should not commit adultery; do you commit adultery? You detest idols; do you rob temples? You take pride in the law; do you dishonor God by breaking it? As it is written, “Because of you the name of God is insulted among the Gentiles.”

Circumcision of the heart

Circumcision is worth something if you keep the law. If you break the law, though, you are as good as uncircumcised. So if an uncircumcised man keeps what the law requires, will God not count him as circumcised? The man who is uncircumcised by birth but carries out the law will judge you, who have the law in writing and are circumcised, yet break the law. For a person is not a Jew because of what is outward, and circumcision is not something outward in the body. No, the one who is a Jew inwardly is the Jew, and the circumcision that counts is of the heart, by the Spirit and not by the letter. That person’s praise comes from God, not from people.

fields.title: Romans 3
fields.body_html:
God is faithful

Then what advantage does the Jew have? What good is circumcision? Much, in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the very words of God. What of it? If some were unfaithful, does their unfaithfulness cancel out God’s faithfulness? Certainly not! Let God be found true, even if every human being is a liar. As it is written, “So that you are shown to be right when you speak, and win your case when you are judged.” But if our wrongdoing brings out God’s righteousness more clearly, what are we to say? Is God unjust, then, when he brings his wrath on us? I am speaking as people do. Certainly not! If that were so, how could God judge the world? But if my falsehood makes God’s truth shine out all the more, to his glory, why am I, too, still judged a sinner? And why not do what some slander us by saying we teach: “Let us do evil so that good may come of it”? Such people deserve their condemnation.

No one is righteous

What then? Do we Jews have an advantage? Not at all. We have already brought the charge that all, Jews and Greeks alike, are under the power of sin. As it is written, “No one is righteous, not even one. No one understands; no one seeks God.” “All have turned away; together they have become useless. No one does what is good, not a single one.” “Their throat is a grave left open; with their tongues they deal in deceit. Snake venom lies behind their lips. Their mouths overflow with cursing and bitter words.” “They rush to shed blood; wherever they go they leave ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have never known.” “The fear of God is nowhere in their sight.”

We know that what the law says is addressed to those who live under the law. It is said so that every mouth will be closed and the whole world will stand accountable to God. No one will be declared righteous before him on the basis of works of the law. What the law does is make sin known.

God’s righteousness through faith

But now God’s righteousness has come to light apart from the law, though the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. It is God’s righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. No one is treated differently. Everyone has sinned, and all come short of God’s glory. Yet they are declared righteous as a free gift, by his grace, through the redemption found in Christ Jesus. God put him forward as the means of atonement, by his blood, to be received through faith. He did this to show his righteousness, since he had passed over the sins committed before, when God held back his judgment. He did it to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he would be righteous and also the one who declares righteous whoever has faith in Jesus.

No room for boasting

So what room is left for boasting? It has been shut out. By what law? A law of works? No, by the law of faith. For we are convinced that a person is declared righteous by faith, apart from works of the law. Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too, since God is one. He will declare the circumcised righteous by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith. Does this faith mean, then, that we do away with the law? Certainly not! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

fields.title: Romans 4
fields.body_html:
Abraham counted righteous by faith

What then are we to say that Abraham, our ancestor by natural descent, has found? Suppose Abraham was declared righteous because of his works: then he would have grounds for boasting, but not in God’s presence. What does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and that was counted to him as righteousness.” A worker’s wages are not counted as grace but as what is owed. But to someone who does no work, yet believes in the God who declares the ungodly righteous, that faith is counted as righteousness. David says the same when he speaks of the happiness of the one whom God counts as righteous apart from works: “How happy are those whose wrongs are forgiven, whose sins are covered over! How happy is the one whose sin the Lord will never count against them!”

Is this blessing, then, only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham’s faith was counted to him as righteousness. Under what circumstances, then, was it counted? Was it after he was circumcised, or before? It was not after, but before. Circumcision was given to him afterward as a sign, a seal on the righteousness that was already his by faith before he was circumcised. In this way he is father to everyone who believes without being circumcised, so that righteousness is counted to them. And he is father to the circumcised as well: not to those who are merely circumcised, but to those who walk the same road of faith our father Abraham walked while still uncircumcised.

The promise comes through faith

The promise that he would inherit the world did not come to Abraham or to his offspring through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. If the heirs are those who rely on the law, faith is made empty and the promise is worthless. The law brings about wrath. But where there is no law, there is no breaking of the law either.

Abraham, the father of us all

So the promise comes through faith, in order that it may rest on grace and stand firm for every one of Abraham’s offspring: not only for those who belong to the law, but also for those who belong to the faith of Abraham, the father of all of us. Scripture says, “I have made you father of many nations.” Before God he is our father, the God he believed, who brings the dead to life and calls into being things that do not exist. Hoping when there was no ground for hope, Abraham believed, and so he became the father of many nations, as God had said to him, “That is how many your offspring will be.” His faith did not weaken when he looked at his own body, as good as dead now that he was about a hundred years old, or at the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not doubt God’s promise or waver in unbelief. Instead he grew strong in faith and gave glory to God, fully convinced that God had the power to carry out what he had promised. That is why “it was counted to him as righteousness.”

Written for us too

The words “it was counted to him” were not written for Abraham alone, but for us as well. It will be counted to us who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was handed over to die because of our trespasses, and he was raised so that we would be declared righteous.

fields.title: Romans 5
fields.body_html:
At peace with God through faith

So now that we have been declared righteous by faith, we are at peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also been brought by faith into this grace where we now stand, and we boast in the hope of sharing God’s glory. More than that, we boast even in our troubles, because we know that trouble leads to endurance, endurance to proven character, and proven character to hope. And hope does not leave us ashamed, for God has given us the Holy Spirit, and through the Spirit his love has flooded our hearts.

God’s love shown while we were sinners

While we were still helpless, at the time God had chosen, Christ died for the ungodly. It is rare for anyone to give their life even for a righteous person; for a good person, perhaps, someone might find the courage to die. But God proves how much he loves us: Christ died for us when we were still sinners. Since we have now been declared righteous by his blood, it is all the more certain that we will be saved through him from God’s wrath. We were enemies of God when the death of his Son reconciled us to him. Now that we are reconciled, it is all the more certain that we will be saved by the Son’s life. More than that, we boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him this reconciliation is now ours.

Through one man sin, through one man grace

Therefore, just as through one man sin came into the world, and death came by sin, and so death reached all people because all sinned— for sin was already in the world before the law was given, but where there is no law, sin is not entered in the account. Even so, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over people whose sin was not like Adam’s breaking of a command. And Adam is a pattern of the one who was to come.

But the trespass and the free gift are not alike. If many died because of one man’s trespass, then far more has God’s grace overflowed to the many, together with the gift given by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ. Nor is the gift like what came through the one man who sinned. The judgment followed one trespass and brought condemnation, but the free gift followed many trespasses and brought acquittal. If death reigned through one man because of that one man’s trespass, it is far more certain that those who receive grace in full measure and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.

So then, as one trespass meant condemnation for all people, so one righteous act means for all people that they are declared righteous and given life. For the disobedience of one man made the many sinners, and in the same way the obedience of the one will make the many righteous. The law came in alongside, so that the trespass would multiply. But where sin multiplied, grace overflowed far beyond it, so that, as sin held its reign through death, grace in turn might reign through righteousness and lead to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

fields.title: Romans 6
fields.body_html:
Dead to sin, alive to God

What then are we to say? Are we to stay on in sin, so that grace may increase all the more? Certainly not! We are people who died to sin; how could we still be living in it? Or have you not grasped that everyone among us who was baptized into Christ Jesus was baptized into his death? So through baptism we were buried with him into death, in order that, as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might live a life that is new.

For if we have grown into one with him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly be one with him in the likeness of his resurrection as well. We know this: our old self was nailed to the cross with him, so that the body of sin would be stripped of its power and we would no longer serve sin as slaves. For anyone who has died is declared free from sin. Now if we died along with Christ, we believe we are also going to share in his life. For we know that Christ, once raised from the dead, does not die any more; death is no longer his master. When he died, he died to sin once and for all; and now that he lives, he lives for God. In the same way, you also are to count yourselves as dead to sin, and as living for God in Christ Jesus.

So do not let sin reign as king in your mortal body, making you obey its desires. Do not keep handing over the parts of your body to sin as weapons for wrongdoing. Instead, hand yourselves over to God, as people who were dead and are now alive, and hand over the parts of your body to God as weapons for righteousness. Sin will not be lord over you, for you do not live under the law but under grace.

Slaves of righteousness

What then? Should we go ahead and sin, since we live under grace and not under the law? Certainly not! Surely you know this: if you put yourselves at someone’s disposal as slaves, ready to obey, then you belong as slaves to the one you obey. That master is either sin, bringing death, or obedience, bringing righteousness. But God be thanked! Once you were slaves of sin, yet you gave wholehearted obedience to the pattern of teaching into whose care you were handed. Freed from sin, you were made slaves of righteousness. I am putting this in everyday human terms because of your natural human weakness. Just as you once handed over the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, which only led to more lawlessness, so now hand them over as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.

Back when sin owned you as slaves, you were free, as far as righteousness was concerned. So what fruit did you get back then from the things that now make you ashamed? Those things end in death. Now, though, freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have fruit that leads to holiness, and its outcome is eternal life. The wages sin pays are death, but God’s free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

fields.title: Romans 7
fields.body_html:
Free from the law

Surely you understand, brothers and sisters, since I am speaking to people who know the law, that the law is master over someone only while that person is alive. Take a married woman: the law binds her to her husband while he is alive. But if he dies, she is set free from the law that tied her to him. So if she joins herself to another man while her husband is still living, people will call her an adulteress. But once her husband has died she is free from the law, and marrying another man does not make her an adulteress.

It is the same with you, my brothers and sisters. Through the body of Christ you were put to death as far as the law is concerned, so that you could be joined to another: to the one who was raised from the dead. And so we can bear fruit for God. When we lived in the flesh, the law stirred up sinful desires in us. They were at work in the parts of our bodies, and what we produced belonged to death. But now we are free from the law. We have died to what once held us fast, so that we serve in the new life of the Spirit, not in the old life of the written letter.

The law and sin

What then are we to say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! But it was the law that taught me what sin is. I would never have recognized wrong desire for what it is unless the law had said, “You shall not covet.” Sin found its opening in the commandment and used it to rouse every kind of wrong desire in me, for without the law sin is dead. There was a time when I lived without the law. Then the commandment arrived, sin woke up and came alive, and I died. The commandment was given for life, yet for me it led to death. Sin found its opening in the commandment, deceived me, and used the commandment to kill me. The law, then, is holy. The commandment is holy, just and good.

Did something good, then, become death to me? Certainly not! Sin was the cause. It used what was good to work death in me, so that sin would be seen for what it really is. Through the commandment sin showed itself sinful past all measure.

Wanting the good, not doing it

We know that the law is spiritual. I, however, am made of flesh, and I have been sold to sin as its slave. What I am doing makes no sense to me. The things I want to do, I fail to do; the things I hate are what I end up doing. But if I do things I do not want to do, that shows I side with the law: I agree that it is good. In that case, I am no longer the one doing it; sin is, the sin that has made its home in me. I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there is nothing good living. Wanting the good is within my reach; doing it is not. I fail to do the good I want, and the evil I do not want is what I carry out. But if I do what I do not want, then I am no longer the one doing it; sin is, the sin that has made its home in me.

This, then, is the law I discover: whenever I set out to do what is good, evil is already there at my side. In my inner self I gladly agree with God’s law. But I see another law in the parts of my body. It is at war with the law of my mind, and it takes me prisoner to the law of sin that is in those parts of my body. Wretched man that I am! Who will set me free from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!

So then, I myself serve God’s law with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh.

fields.title: Romans 8
fields.body_html:
Set free by the Spirit of life

So then, those who are in Christ Jesus now face no sentence of condemnation. For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit who gives life has freed you from the law of sin and death. The law was powerless, since the flesh had left it weak. So God acted. He sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, as an offering for sin, and in the flesh he passed sentence on sin. He did this so that the law’s righteous requirement would be fully met in us, who conduct our lives by the Spirit and not by the flesh. Those who are under the rule of the flesh have their minds fixed on the concerns of the flesh, but those under the rule of the Spirit, on the concerns of the Spirit. The outlook of the flesh means death, but the outlook of the Spirit means life and peace. That is because the outlook of the flesh is at war with God. It does not bow to God’s law, and in fact it is not able to. People who are in the flesh have no power to please God.

But you are not in the flesh; you are in the Spirit, if God’s Spirit really does live in you. If anyone lacks the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his. But if Christ is in you, the body is marked for death because of sin, but the Spirit is life for you because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead has made a home in you, then God, who raised Christ Jesus from the dead, will bring your mortal bodies to life as well, because his Spirit lives in you.

God’s children by the Spirit

So then, brothers and sisters, we are under an obligation, but not to the flesh, to live as the flesh dictates. If you live as the flesh dictates, you are headed for death. But if by the Spirit you keep putting the body’s practices to death, you will live. Those whom God’s Spirit is leading are God’s children. What you received was not a spirit of slavery that would put you back under fear. You received the Spirit of adoption as children, and in the Spirit we call out, “Abba, Father!” The Spirit himself joins our own spirit in testifying that we are God’s children. If we are children, we are also heirs. We are God’s heirs, and we inherit alongside Christ, if we suffer together with him so that we will also be glorified together with him.

Creation waits to be set free

I have weighed it up: what we suffer in this present time does not begin to balance the glory that is going to be revealed to us. The created world cranes its neck in longing, waiting for God’s children to be revealed. Creation was made subject to futility. This was not its own choice; it was because of the one who subjected it. Yet there was hope: creation itself will also be released from its slavery to decay and will enter the freedom that comes with the glory of God’s children. We know that all creation, to this very day, groans as one and suffers the pains of giving birth together. And not creation alone. We ourselves, who have the Spirit as the first share of the harvest, also groan within ourselves while we long for our adoption as children, when our body will be redeemed. It was in hope that we were saved. But a hope that is already in sight is no hope at all. Who goes on hoping for what is already in front of them? But if what we hope for is something we do not yet see, we keep waiting for it with endurance.

The Spirit pleads for us

In the same way, the Spirit also lends a hand in our weakness. What we should pray for, and how, we do not know. But the Spirit himself pleads on our behalf, with groans that no words carry. And God, who looks deep into hearts, knows what the Spirit intends, because the Spirit pleads for God’s holy people in line with what God wants.

Called according to God’s purpose

We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good. They are the ones called in keeping with his purpose. Those God knew beforehand he also marked out beforehand to be shaped into the image of his Son, so that the Son would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. And those he marked out beforehand, he also called. Those he called, he also declared righteous. And those he declared righteous, he also glorified.

If God is on our side

So what is our response to all this? If God is on our side, who can stand against us? God did not hold back even his own Son, but handed him over for us all. How could he fail, then, to give us everything along with him as a free gift? Who will bring any accusation against those God has chosen? God is the one who declares them righteous. Who is going to condemn them? Christ is the one who died; still more, he was raised, and he is at the right hand of God, where he pleads on our behalf. Who can tear us away from the love of Christ? Trouble, or anguish, or persecution? Hunger, or lack of clothing, or danger, or the sword? As it is written, “On your account we are being killed the whole day through; we are looked on as sheep for the butcher.” But in all of this we are winning, and winning by far, through the one who loved us. For I am fully persuaded that not death and not life, not angels and not rulers, not what is here now and not what is yet to come, not any powers, not what is high above and not what is deep below, nor any other created thing, will be able to cut us off from God’s love, which is ours in Christ Jesus our Lord.

fields.title: Romans 9
fields.body_html:
Paul’s grief for Israel

I am telling the truth in Christ; I am not lying. My conscience, in the Holy Spirit, bears witness with me that my sorrow is great and the pain in my heart never stops. I could even wish that I myself were under a curse, cut off from Christ, on behalf of my brothers and sisters, my own people by human descent. They are Israelites. Theirs is the adoption as God’s children, theirs the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship and the promises. The patriarchs are theirs, and from them, by human descent, comes Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

God’s word has not failed

But this does not mean that God’s word has failed. For not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel. Nor are they all Abraham’s children just because they are his descendants. Rather, “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be named.” This means that it is not the children born by natural descent who are God’s children. It is the children of the promise who are counted as Abraham’s offspring. For this is what the promise said: “At this time I will come back, and a son will be born to Sarah.” And that is not all. Rebecca also conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac. The children were not yet born and had done nothing good or bad. Yet so that God’s purpose in choosing might stand, a purpose that rests not on works but on the one who calls, Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” As it is written, “I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated.”

Is God unjust?

What then are we to say? Is there injustice on God’s part? Certainly not! For God says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whomever I show compassion.” So it is not a matter of what a person wants or how hard a person strives, but of God, who shows mercy. For Scripture says to Pharaoh, “This is the very reason I raised you up: to display my power in you, and so that my name would be made known through the whole earth.” So then God has mercy on whomever he chooses, and he hardens whomever he chooses.

The potter and the clay

So you will say to me, “Why does God still find fault, then?” For who can stand against his will? But who are you, a mere human being, to answer back to God? Will what was shaped say to the one who shaped it, “Why did you make me this way?” Has the potter no right over the clay? From one and the same lump he may make one pot for honored use and another for common use. What if God, wanting to show his wrath and to make his power known, has borne with great patience the vessels of wrath, made ready for destruction? What if he did this to make known the riches of his glory to the vessels of mercy, which he prepared in advance for glory, that is, to us, whom he has called not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles? As he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not loved I will call ‘loved.’” “And in the place where they were told, ‘You are not my people,’ that is where they will be called children of the living God.” And Isaiah cries out about Israel: “Though the people of Israel are as many as the grains of sand by the sea, the remnant will be saved.” “For on the earth the Lord will carry out his sentence, fully and without delay.” And as Isaiah said earlier, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us some descendants, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”

Israel and the stone of stumbling

What then are we to say? That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have obtained it, the righteousness that comes by faith. But Israel, who pursued a law that held out righteousness, did not reach that law. Why not? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as though it came by works. They stumbled over the stone that makes people stumble, as it is written, “See, I am setting in Zion a stone to stumble on, a rock that makes them fall, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

fields.title: Romans 10
fields.body_html:
The righteousness that comes by faith

Brothers and sisters, what my heart longs for, and what I ask God for them, is that they may be saved. I can vouch for them that they are eager for God, but their eagerness is not guided by real understanding. They did not recognize the righteousness of God, and in trying to set up a righteousness of their own, they would not submit to the righteousness that comes from God. For Christ is the end of the law, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes. Moses writes this about the righteousness that comes from the law: “The person who does it will live by it.” But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks like this: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down). Or, “Who will go down into the abyss?” (that is, to bring Christ back up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is close to you, on your lips and in your heart.” This is the message of faith that we proclaim. If you declare with your lips that Jesus is Lord, and in your heart believe that God raised him from the dead, then you will be saved. For people believe with the heart, and this leads to righteousness; they confess with the mouth, and this leads to salvation. For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” Here there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for one and the same Lord is Lord over everyone, and he gives generously to all who call on him. For “all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

How will they hear?

How, then, are they to call on him if they have not believed in him? And how are they to believe in him if they have never heard him? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming? And how are people to proclaim it unless they are sent? As it is written, “How lovely are the feet of those who bring the good news of good things!” But not all have obeyed the gospel. Isaiah asks, “Lord, who has believed what we have told?” So faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ.

Israel heard and refused

But I ask, is it possible that they did not hear? Indeed they did: “Their voice went out to the whole earth, and their words to the farthest parts of the world.” Again I ask, is it possible that Israel did not understand? First, Moses says, “I will stir you to jealousy through those who are not a nation, and through a nation without understanding I will provoke your anger.” Then Isaiah dares to say, “I was found by people who were not looking for me; I showed myself to those who never asked for me.” But about Israel he says, “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who disobey and argue back.”

fields.title: Romans 11
fields.body_html:
The remnant of Israel

So I ask: has God rejected his people? Certainly not! I myself am an Israelite, descended from Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what Scripture says in the story of Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel? “Lord, they have killed your prophets and demolished your altars. I alone am left, and now they are trying to take my life.” But what was God’s answer to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand people who have not bent the knee to Baal.” In the same way, at the present time too there is a remnant, chosen by grace. And if it is by grace, it does not come from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. What then? Israel did not obtain what it was seeking. Those God chose obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, “God has given them a spirit of numbness, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, to this very day.” And David says, “May their table turn into a snare and a net, a stumbling block and a just penalty for them. May their eyes grow dark so that they cannot see, and keep their backs bent forever.”

Israel’s stumbling and the Gentiles’ salvation

So I ask: did they stumble so as to fall for good? Certainly not! Rather, through their wrongdoing salvation has come to the Gentiles, so that Israel would become jealous. Now if their wrongdoing means riches for the world, and their loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches their fullness will bring!

Now I am speaking to you who are Gentiles. So since I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I make much of my ministry, in the hope that somehow I may make my own flesh and blood jealous and save some of them. For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean? Nothing less than life from the dead! If the portion of dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole batch; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

The olive tree and its branches

Now if some of the branches were broken off, and you, though a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among them and now share in the rich root of the olive tree, do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, remember: you do not hold up the root; the root holds you up. Then you will say, “Branches were broken off to let me be grafted in.” That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand firm by faith. Do not be proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the branches that grew naturally on the tree, he will not spare you either. Notice, then, both the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but God’s kindness toward you, as long as you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off. And they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them back in. After all, if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree and grafted, against nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more readily will these natural branches be grafted back into their own olive tree!

All Israel will be saved

Brothers and sisters, I want you to understand this mystery, so that you will not think yourselves wise: a hardening has come upon part of Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in. And in this way all Israel will be saved. As it is written, “Out of Zion will come the Deliverer; he will turn ungodliness away from Jacob.” “And this will be my covenant with them, when I take their sins away.” As far as the gospel is concerned, they are enemies for your sake; but as far as God’s choice is concerned, they are loved because of the patriarchs. For the gifts and the call of God can never be taken back. Once you were disobedient to God, but now you have been shown mercy because of their disobedience. In the same way they have now been disobedient, so that by the mercy God has shown you, they too may now be shown mercy. For God has locked everyone up together in disobedience, so that he may show mercy to everyone.

Praise to God’s wisdom

How deep are the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How impossible to search out his judgments, and how impossible to trace his ways!

For “who has known the mind of the Lord?” “Or who has been his counselor?” “Or who has given him anything first and must be paid back?” For all things are from him and through him and for him. To him be glory forever! Amen.

fields.title: Romans 12
fields.body_html:
A living sacrifice

So, brothers and sisters, I appeal to you by the mercies of God: offer your bodies to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to him. That is your reasonable worship. Do not let this present age press you into its mold, but be changed through and through as your mind is made new. Then you will be able to test and recognize the will of God: what is good and pleasing and perfect.

One body, many gifts

By the grace given to me I tell each one of you: do not rate yourself higher than you should. Let your thinking be sober and sensible instead, in keeping with the measure of faith that God has assigned to each of you. We have many parts in a single body, and the parts do not all have the same task. In the same way, many as we are, we are one body in Christ, and each of us is a part that belongs to all the others. We have gifts that differ, according to the grace given to us. If someone’s gift is prophecy, they should prophesy in proportion to their faith. If it is serving, they should give themselves to serving; the one who teaches, to teaching; the one who encourages, to encouraging. The one who shares should share generously; the one who leads, with eagerness; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

Love without pretense

Let your love be real, with no pretense. Loathe evil and stick to what is good. Love one another warmly, as brothers and sisters in one family; take the lead in honoring one another. Never let your eagerness flag; be on fire in the Spirit; serve the Lord. Let your hope keep you rejoicing; hold out under trouble; keep at prayer. Share with God’s holy people in their needs, and be eager to welcome guests. Bless the people who persecute you. Bless them, and do not curse them. Share the joy of those who are glad, and the tears of those who weep. Be of one mind toward each other. Do not aim at lofty things, but be glad to go along with people of low position. Do not count yourselves wise. Do not pay anyone back with evil for the evil done to you. Plan ahead to do what everyone recognizes as good. If it can be done, and so far as it lies with you, keep peace with everyone. Dear friends, never avenge yourselves. Step aside and let God’s wrath do its work, for it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay,” says the Lord. Instead, if your enemy is hungry, give them food; if they are thirsty, give them something to drink. By doing this you will pile burning coals on their head. Do not let evil defeat you; defeat evil with good.

fields.title: Romans 13
fields.body_html:
Living under governing authorities

Everyone must submit to the authorities who govern, because no authority exists except by God’s doing, and the authorities that are in place have been put there by God. So anyone who sets themselves against the authority is standing against what God has ordered, and those who take that stand will bring judgment on themselves. Rulers are not something to fear when you do what is good, only when you do what is wrong. Would you like to have no fear of the one in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive its approval. For the ruler is God’s servant, working for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, because the ruler does not carry the sword for nothing. The ruler is God’s servant, one who avenges and brings wrath on anyone who does wrong. So you must submit, not only to escape wrath but also for the sake of conscience. This is the reason you also pay taxes: those in authority serve God in a public office, and they give themselves to this very task. Pay everyone what you owe them: taxes to the one who collects taxes, customs to the one who collects customs, respect to the one who is owed respect, honor to the one who is owed honor.

Love fulfills the law

Do not stay in debt to anyone, except for the debt of love you owe one another. Whoever loves another person has fulfilled the law. Take the commandments “Do not commit adultery,” “Do not murder,” “Do not steal,” “Do not covet”: these, and whatever other commandment there is, are gathered up in this one saying: “You must love your neighbor as you love yourself.” Love does no harm to a neighbor, and so love is what fulfills the law.

The day is near

Do this because you know what time it is: it is already time for you to wake up out of sleep. Our salvation is closer now than it was when we first believed. The night is almost over; the day is close. So let us take off the deeds that belong to darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us live decently, as people do in the daytime: not in wild parties and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and shameless excess, not in quarrels and envy. Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ like clothing, and do not make plans to satisfy the desires of the flesh.

fields.title: Romans 14
fields.body_html:
The weak and the strong

Welcome anyone whose faith is weak, but not in order to quarrel over their opinions. One person believes it is right to eat anything, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables. The one who eats must not look down on the one who abstains, and the one who abstains must not pass judgment on the one who eats, because God has welcomed that person. Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? It is to their own master that they stand or fall. And they will stand, because the Lord has the power to keep them standing.

One person regards one day as more important than another, while someone else regards every day as the same. Each person must be fully convinced in their own mind. Whoever observes the day does so for the Lord. Those who eat do so for the Lord, since they give thanks to God; and those who abstain do so for the Lord, and they too give thanks to God.

For not one of us lives for ourselves, and not one of us dies for ourselves. If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. So, living or dying, we belong to the Lord. This is why Christ died and came to life: so that he would be Lord of both the dead and the living.

We will all stand before God

You, then, why do you pass judgment on your brother or sister? Or you, why do you look down on your brother or sister? We will all stand before God’s judgment seat. For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bend before me, and every tongue will openly acknowledge God.” So each of us will have to give an account of ourselves.

Do not make another believer stumble

So let us stop judging one another. Use your judgment for this instead: never to put a stumbling block or a snare in the way of a brother or sister. I know, and in the Lord Jesus I am fully persuaded, that nothing is unclean in itself. But if someone considers a thing unclean, then for that person it is unclean. If your brother or sister is being hurt by what you eat, you are no longer walking in the way of love. Do not let what you eat bring ruin on someone for whom Christ died. So do not let the good thing you have be slandered. For the kingdom of God is not about eating and drinking. It is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Anyone who serves Christ in this way pleases God and wins the approval of others. So let us pursue whatever makes for peace and whatever builds one another up. Do not pull down God’s work just for the sake of food. All food is clean, it is true, but it is wrong for anyone to eat in a way that makes another stumble. It is right not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything else that makes your brother or sister stumble or fall or become weak. Whatever faith you have about these things, keep it between yourself and God. Blessed are those who do not condemn themselves by what they approve. But anyone who has doubts and eats anyway stands condemned, because the eating does not come from faith. Whatever does not come from faith is sin.

fields.title: Romans 15
fields.body_html:
Bearing with the weak, as Christ did

Those of us who are strong have a duty to carry the weaknesses of those who lack strength, instead of living to please ourselves. Each of us should please our neighbor, aiming at what is good for them and what builds them up. For even Christ did not please himself. Instead, as it is written, “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.” Everything that was written in earlier times was written to teach us. It was written so that we might have hope, as we endure and as the Scriptures encourage us. May God, who gives endurance and encouragement, grant you to live in harmony with one another, as Christ Jesus would have you, so that together, with one voice, you may give glory to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The Gentiles glorify God for his mercy

So welcome one another, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised for the sake of God’s truth, to make good the promises given to the patriarchs, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “That is why I will praise you among the Gentiles and sing praises to your name.” And again it says, “Rejoice, you Gentiles, together with his people.” And again, “All you Gentiles, praise the Lord; let all the peoples sing his praise.” And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, the one who rises to rule over the Gentiles; the Gentiles will set their hope on him.” May the God of hope fill you with joy and peace of every kind as you believe, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you overflow with hope.

Paul’s work as a minister to the Gentiles

My brothers and sisters, I myself am convinced about you: you are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able to counsel one another. Yet on some points I have written to you quite boldly, to remind you of them again. I have done so because of the grace God gave me to be a minister of Christ Jesus for the Gentiles. I serve the gospel of God like a priest, so that the Gentiles may become an offering that God accepts, made holy by the Holy Spirit. So in Christ Jesus I have reason to boast of my service to God. I will not venture to speak of anything but what Christ has done through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, through what I have said and done, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit. So I have completed the preaching of the gospel of Christ in a wide circle from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. My aim has been to preach the gospel where Christ was not yet known, so that I would not build on a foundation someone else had laid. Instead, as it is written, “Those who were never told of him will see, and those who never heard will understand.”

Paul’s plans: Jerusalem, Rome and Spain

That is why I have so often been prevented from coming to you. But now there is no more room for my work in these regions, and for many years I have longed to come to you when I travel to Spain. I hope to see you as I pass through, and to have you help me on my way there, after I have enjoyed your company for a while. Right now, though, I am on my way to Jerusalem to serve God’s holy people. For the churches of Macedonia and Achaia were glad to share what they had with the poor among God’s holy people in Jerusalem. They were glad to do it, and they really do owe it to them. If the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to serve them with material help. So once I have finished this task and made sure they have received this fruit, I will set out for Spain and visit you on the way. I know that when I do come to you, I will come with the full blessing of Christ.

A request for prayer

Brothers and sisters, I appeal to you by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love the Spirit gives: join me in my struggle through your prayers to God for me. Ask that I may be rescued from those in Judea who refuse to believe, and that God’s holy people in Jerusalem will welcome the help I bring them. Then, if God wills, I can come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

fields.title: Romans 16
fields.body_html:
Paul commends Phoebe

I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a deacon of the church in Cenchreae. I ask you to welcome her in the Lord in the way God’s holy people should, and to stand by her in anything she may need from you. She has been a patron to many, and to me as well.

Greetings to believers in Rome

Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus. They put their own necks on the line for my life, and it is not only I who thank them: all the churches of the Gentiles do too. Greet also the church that meets in their house. Greet my dear friend Epaenetus, the first of the harvest for Christ in Asia. Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my fellow Jews, who were in prison with me. They are prominent among the apostles, and they were in Christ earlier than I was. Greet Ampliatus, whom I love in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our co-worker in Christ, and my dear friend Stachys. Greet Apelles, who has been tested and found true in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, my fellow Jew. Greet those in the household of Narcissus who belong to the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, women who work hard in the Lord. Greet dear Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and greet his mother, who has also been a mother to me. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all God’s holy people who are with them.

Greet one another with a holy kiss.

All the churches of Christ send you greetings.

A warning against those who divide

Brothers and sisters, I urge you to keep an eye on those who stir up divisions and put stumbling blocks in people’s way, against the teaching you were taught. Keep away from them. People like this are not serving our Lord Christ; they are serving their own stomachs. With smooth talk and fine-sounding words they lead astray the hearts of trusting people. Everyone has heard of your obedience, and so I am glad about you. Still, I want you to be wise in what is good and to keep yourselves untouched by what is evil. And before long the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

Greetings from Paul’s companions

Timothy, my co-worker, sends you greetings, and so do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow Jews. I, Tertius, the one who wrote this letter down, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, and so does our brother Quartus.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching about Jesus Christ, in keeping with the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but is now disclosed and, through the prophetic Scriptures and by the command of the eternal God, has been made known to all the nations to bring about the obedience of faith— to the only wise God be glory forever and ever through Jesus Christ! Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching about Jesus Christ, in keeping with the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but is now disclosed and, through the prophetic Scriptures and by the command of the eternal God, has been made known to all the nations to bring about the obedience of faith— to the only wise God be glory forever and ever through Jesus Christ! Amen.

— Romans 16:25–27

Romans ends as it began. In its first paragraph Paul says he received grace and apostleship “to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations”; in its last sentence the mystery kept secret for long ages has been made known to all the nations “to bring about the obedience of faith”. Everything in between, the guilt of all, the gift of righteousness, the life of the Spirit, the grief over Israel and the welcome at the table, lies between those two phrases. And the whole of it ends, as Paul’s great arguments always do, in praise.

Where the letter points

It points, first, to God. Romans is often read as a book about salvation, and it is. But when Paul reaches the end of his hardest argument, in chapter 11, he does not sum it up. He worships:

How deep are the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How impossible to search out his judgments, and how impossible to trace his ways! For all things are from him and through him and for him. To him be glory forever! Amen.

— Romans 11:33, 36

A reader who finishes Romans knowing more doctrine but loving God no more has missed what Paul was doing. The argument is meant to end on our knees.

It points, second, to a people. The letter that tells us God declares the ungodly righteous also tells the strong to carry the weaknesses of those who lack strength, and greets Phoebe, Prisca, Junia and Rufus’s mother by name. Justification by faith, in Romans, is never a private arrangement between one soul and God. It makes Jews and Gentiles into one family, who must now learn to eat together.

And it points outward, to the nations. Paul wrote, after all, because he was on his way to Spain. In chapter 10 he asks, “how are they to believe in him if they have never heard him?”, and the question has sent missionaries out ever since. He did reach Rome, though not as he planned: arrested in Jerusalem, he came as a prisoner, and Acts leaves him there, preaching in his rented lodgings, without hindrance. Whether he ever reached Spain no one knows for certain. Clement, writing from the church in Rome a generation later, says that Paul taught righteousness to the whole world and reached the farthest bounds of the West.

Where to go from here

Romans has drawn out the best of the church’s preachers and teachers for as long as there has been a church, and many of them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • Through the whole letter. John Chrysostom’s Homilies on Romans, preached at Antioch, and John Calvin’s Commentary on Romans, which Calvin called a way into all of Scripture.
  • On sin and the gift of righteousness (chapters 1–4). Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s The Wrath of God (1:18), John Wesley’s The Circumcision of the Heart (2:29), Charles H. Spurgeon’s Justification by Grace (3:24) and his All of Grace, and George Whitefield’s The Lord Our Righteousness (on Jeremiah 23:6). For the man who found the gospel in 1:17, The Key Teachings of Martin Luther and Luther’s own First Principles of the Reformation.
  • On peace with God (chapter 5). Alexander Maclaren’s Let Us Have Peace, which follows the other reading of 5:1, his The Sources of Hope and What Proves God’s Love; Thomas Chalmers’s The Sure Warrant of a Believer’s Hope; Christmas Evans’s Fall and Recovery of Man; and A. B. Simpson’s Grace Abounding.
  • On sin and the new life (chapters 6–8). John Owen wrote on these chapters more searchingly than almost anyone: The Dominion of Sin and Grace (6:14), Indwelling Sin in Believers (chapter 7), The Mortification of Sin in Believers (8:13) and The Grace and Duty of Being Spiritually Minded (8:6).
  • On Romans 8. Thomas Watson’s All Things for Good (8:28); two sermons called The Witness of the Spirit (8:16), by John Wesley and by Maclaren; Charles G. Finney’s The Spirit of Prayer (8:26–27); Maclaren’s Sons and Heirs and The Gift That Brings All Gifts; John Newton’s If God Be for Us; and Simpson’s More Than Conquerors.
  • On Israel, the nations and the gospel’s reach (chapters 9–11). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s Our Duty to Israel and Believers Not Ashamed, both on 1:16; Spurgeon’s A Simple Sermon for Seeking Souls (10:13); and Simpson’s The Logic of Missions (10:14–15).
  • The lives it changed, and the church it was written to. Augustine of Hippo’s Confessions, whose eighth book ends in the garden at Milan; The Journal of John Wesley, with the evening at Aldersgate; and two letters from the generations after Paul: The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, sent from the church in Rome, and Ignatius of Antioch’s letter to it, in The Epistles of Ignatius and His Life’s Story.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Romans in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read Romans again, and perhaps to read it aloud, as Phoebe’s hearers first heard it, all at once. The argument that seemed so hard the first time will begin to sound like what it is: good news, set out by a man who could not stop marvelling at it. And Paul’s prayer for the Romans may become his prayer for you:

May the God of hope fill you with joy and peace of every kind as you believe, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you overflow with hope.

— Romans 15:13
